content.title: Author Response [Part 2]
content.comment:
Q4: In Fig.6, one can observe that only two weights are relatively large - what this means? how does this affect performance?

R4: This helps explain how the branching architecture works empirically. Fig.6 shows that, instead of simply averaging the outputs from each branch, each branch is assigned with either a large weight (close to 1) or very small weight (close to 0). In general, only 1-2 (out of 10) branches are assigned with meaningful weights while the others are 'killed'. Since all the branches are trained with the same objective, the only difference is that their initial weights are determined randomly. Consequently, such a behavior illustrates how network weights are initialized can impact the performance, and it is important to use branching to reduce the variations caused by the random initialization. In contrast, Fig.4 shows that by simply applying an average ensemble over VLM+RSA does not improve performance significantly, as the impact brought in by random weight initializations are not mitigated.

Q5: it is claimed that "From Fig. 7, one can observe that it tends to significantly under-estimate", why? it seems that there has over-estimate and
under-estimate in Fig.7.

R5: AR ensemble's predictions are shown in the 1st row of Fig. 7, where x-axis shows the true returns and y-axis shows the predicted returns. It can be observed that for Hopper-M-E, Ant-M-E and Walker2d-M-E that a majority of AR's predictions fall below the 45-degree (y=x) line, which shows that AR in general under-estimate policies' performance. The high-performing policies are located to the right-end of x-axis, where very few points are above the 45-degree line; this shows that AR under-estimates most of the high-performing policies. From Fig. 10 and 11 it can be seen that AR could not distinguish the performance of most policies over the Halfcheetah environments, as the predictions mostly form a horizontal line.

Q6: in eq.(3), why a diagnal Gaussian is chosen to model the latent transition model? It could be over-simplified in some complex enironment.

R6: We chose diagonal Gaussian by assuming that little-to-none correlations existed across different dimensions of the states. If correlation exists, one could project the states onto orthogonal basis (e.g., using principal component analysis) such that the non-diagonal elements of the covariance matrix will be zeros. We thank the reviewer for pointing this out, and have clarified the assumption by adding a footnote in section 2.2 (highlighted in blue). 

We would appreciate the reviewer to follow up with any further comments, or to update the review if the comments above are sufficiently addressed. We sincerely thank the reviewer for the time and patience devoted to the review process.

content.title: Author Response [Part 1]
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer's comments. Please find our responses point-by-point below.

Q1: technical novelty is limited: the proposed method is basically a straightforward extention to the VAE model in the sense that the latent variable is extended to a sequence of latent variables modeled, where both encoder and decoder is implemented with LSTMs.

R1: VLBM is significantly different from classic VAEs from two perspectives. First, **a vanilla VAE learns a static (time-invariant) latent space of representations over inputs** (e.g., images of cats and dogs) and generate synthetic images that present similar characteristics. However, they are not capable of capturing dynamical transitions over time, nor being conditioned on other variables that are in the real number space (e.g., actions). In contrast, VLBM captures the MDP's overall **temporal transition dynamics** over the latent space, and to facilitate this it is designed to be **conditioned on the actions (in real number space) resulted in by different target policies**. Given these two factors, the ELBO for training VLBM is derived from the scratch (equation 7 and Appendix D), which also appears to be non-trivial. Second, to allow VLBM to learn as much from a fixed set of offline training data collected over unknown behavioral policies, RSA and branching techniques are introduced which allow encoders to learn disentangled representations (Fig. 8 and Appendix C) and decoders to roll out future states accurately.


Q2: The main concern of this paper is how to train a better transition model, but why this is the core issue of OPE needs further explanation. I think that it's better to evaluate the presented method across more model-based RL applications rather than OPE.

R2: Model-based OPE can facilitate many important applications by itself, such as demonstrating the safety and efficacy of RL-based medical device controllers before deployments in clinical trials. For example, it can estimate how a surgical robot would react to a few critical states in a surgery that are critical for the success, without the need of deploying to patients directly. Moreover, as stated in the paper introducing the AR model [1] that OPE can better help trace the source of improvements back to model design factors, as opposed to policy optimization where the performance is also dependent on how the optimization technique is chosen and configured, e.g., model-based ones such as model predictive control (MPC), or model-free ones such as actor-critic over the model rollouts. **We have updated the introduction section regarding this, with changes highlighted in blue.** However, this is a great question that points out the future works that can be built on top of VLBM. For example, VLBM could be extended to replace the critic network in actor-critic methods, which estimates the expected return from a given state-action pair, as opposed to the OPE case where we focus on estimating returns from the initial states.

Q3: typos: In formula (4), the left side doesn't contain a_{t}, but the right side contain a_{t}.

R3: Thank you for pointing this out. As discussed in the line below (4), the action $a_t$ is conditioned on the target policy $\pi$ and $s_t$, where we missed to add $\pi$ as part of the conditions in (4). This is now corrected.

[1] Zhang, Michael R. et al. "Autoregressive Dynamics Models for Offline Policy Evaluation and Optimization." ICLR 2021.

content.title: Thank you for getting back to us. More justifications.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for getting back to us. We thought it would be helpful to provide more justifications for the points above, to potentially prevent any misunderstandings. 

In regards to (1) made by the reviewer above, the benchmark we used contain two different suite of environments (Mujoco and Adroit) where each one is associated with different tasks with training trajectories collected by various behavioral policies. **Moreover, as reported in Tables 7 and 8, the size of training data varies dramatically across tasks.** For example, Pen-human, Door-human, Hammer-human and Relocate-Human only provide 5k-10k transitions for training, which is considered tiny scale as such environments usually have 30+ dimensional states and 200 steps horizon (**roughly 25-50 trajectories in total**). In comparison, Ant-medium-replay, Halfcheetah-medium-replay, Walker2d-medium-replay and Hopper-medium-replay provides 200k-400k transitions in the training dataset which can be considered as medium-scaled dataset, while some other tasks are associated with 1million+ transitions that are large scale. **From tables 1-6 it can be observed that VLBM is also in lead of the performance in the tasks with small/medium-scaled training datasets.**

As for (2), for model-based methods to capture rewards, the prerequisite would be to model and learn the environmental transition dynamics accurately **from offline data**. As discussed in the related works section, though there exist some works that use variational bayes methods to capture environmental dynamics, such as Dreamers[1,2] and SLAC[3], *they require the data to be collected online*. Moreover, the ablation baseline, VLM, is a generalization of such methods, and results empirically show that such variational models are not capable of estimating the returns accurately. As a result, we introduced the **RSA and branching architecture** that allows variational models to better capture the dynamics over offline data. Following [1,2,3], as well as another model-based OPE work [4], we justified our method extensively with empirical studies in lieu of providing theoretical bounds.

Again, we sincerely thank the reviewer for the efforts spent toward the discussion, allowing the paper to be thoroughly evaluated.

[1] Hafner, Danijar, Timothy Lillicrap, Jimmy Ba, and Mohammad Norouzi. "Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2019.

[2] Hafner, Danijar, Timothy P. Lillicrap, Mohammad Norouzi, and Jimmy Ba. "Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020.

[3] Lee, Alex X., Anusha Nagabandi, Pieter Abbeel, and Sergey Levine. "Stochastic latent actor-critic: Deep reinforcement learning with a latent variable model." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 741-752.

[4] Zhang, Michael R., Tom Le Paine, Ofir Nachum, Cosmin Paduraru, George Tucker, Ziyu Wang, and Mohammad Norouzi. "Autoregressive dynamics models for offline policy evaluation and optimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.13877 (2021).

content.title: Author Response.
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for following up with another 2 insightful questions. Please see our detailed responses below.

*Response to question 1 above*

Given the space limits, Figure. 4 appears to be pretty compact, and it might not be very straightforward to tell the degree of performance improvements over the bar plot. So in the table below we summarize the percentage improvements made by pairwise comparison between VLM, VLM+RSA and VLBM. In general, it can be observed that VLM+RSA did significantly improves over VLM, and VLBM additionally improves over VLM+RSA by similar margins. Such a finding suggests that both RSA and the branching architecture we proposed lead to the improvements made by VLBM. Please also note that **Figure 8 and Appendix B illustrated empirically how RSA can help formulate an expressive and disentangled latent space from which the transition dynamics of the environments are captured**, allowing the model to capture the underlying dynamics and roll out future states and rewards accurately.

|                 | Rank Ant | Rank Halfcheetah | Rank Walker2d | Rank Hopper | Regret@1 Ant | Regret@1 Halfcheetah | Regret@1 Walker2d | Regret@1 Hopper | MAE Ant | MAE Halfcheetah | MAE Walker2d | MAE Hopper |
|-----------------|----------|------------------|---------------|-------------|--------------|----------------------|-------------------|-----------------|---------|-----------------|--------------|------------|
| VLM+RSA vs VLM  | 28.81%   | 19.62%           | 50.00%        | 50.38%      | 20.69%       | 21.33%               | 38.64%            | 1.95%           | 1.05%   | 4.12%           | 11.01%       | 4.14%      |
| VLBM vs VLM+RSA | 58.77%   | 18.01%           | 23.75%        | 41.00%      | 62.32%       | 23.73%               | 59.26%            | 74.83%          | 20.07%  | 11.18%          | 7.39%        | 1.42%      |
| VLBM vs VLM     | 104.52%  | 41.15%           | 85.63%        | 112.03%     | 70.11%       | 40.00%               | 75.00%            | 75.32%          | 20.90%  | 14.83%          | 17.58%       | 2.66%      |

*Response to question 2 above*

Halfcheetah, Door, Hammer and Relocate environments have fixed total steps (2,000 steps for Halfcheetah and 200 for the other three). However, for Ant, Hopper, Walker2d and Pen (2,000 max steps for Ant, Hopper, Walker2d and 200 for Pen), an episode may be terminated early if the states meet specific constraints, resulting in varied trajectory lengths (over different runs). In Appendix D we introduced in details how such 'early termination' behavior is captured. In general, Figures 4 and 5 showed that VLBM achieved top performance regardless the environmental horizon length. We believe that this benefits from enforcing over a compact latent space ($p(z_{t}|z_{t-1},a_{t-1})$) the environmental transitions *over the entire horizon*, as opposed to one-step-look-ahead models (e.g., the AR baseline [1]) where the predicted $\hat s_{t+1}$ is directly conditioned on the prediction from the last step $\hat s_t$. Moreover, previous research [1] and the DOPE benchmark [2] both showed that even feedforward and AR models adapted to the OPE problem lead to more promising results over model-free OPE methods in general. **In this paper, we showed that variational bayes models had made it even further, and we hope that our paper could spark more model-based OPE research along the line in the future**, as it can be potentially leveraged as building blocks for solving other challenges as well, such as sparse rewards, as mentioned by the reviewer.


We are truly grateful for the thoughtful comments provided by the reviewer, and please do not hesitate to let us know if any other clarifications are needed. 


[1] Zhang, Michael R., Thomas Paine, Ofir Nachum, Cosmin Paduraru, George Tucker, and Mohammad Norouzi. "Autoregressive Dynamics Models for Offline Policy Evaluation and Optimization." In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020.

[2] Fu, Justin et al. "Benchmarks for Deep Off-Policy Evaluation." ICLR 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes the application of recurrent world model to the task of off-policy evaluation (OPE) in offline RL setting. As contributions, the paper identifies two empirical techniques to help improve performance in the offline ODE setting: (1) recurrent state alignment (RSA); (2) branching architecture. Finally, experiment results show improvement over baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
=== Strengths ===

The paper seems to propose an interesting application of learning recurrent world model for the purpose of offline ODE. Intriguingly, applying such world model technique does not work optimally out-of-the-box, and as the authors suggest in the paper, would require additional techniques to work better. The paper identifies such important elements as the RSA loss and proposes the novel branching architecture, which can be useful for future investigation in the model-based RL for OPE in general. Experiment results also seem solid.

=== Weakness ===

I think a major weakness of the paper lies in its conceptual contribution. One central question is: since all the tasks being evaluated are Mujoco continuous controls or Adroit tasks, arguably the environments are almost fully Markovian, then what is the principal reason why using a recurrent model works better than just using a Markovian world model? This is a key motivational question not addressed enough by the paper. I will expand more in the following.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
=== Clarity ===

The paper is written quite clearly.

=== Quality ===

The paper has good writing quality and has clear presentations of experiment results. The paper also has good technical quality in terms of empirical contributions, but may have flaws regarding its motivational and conceptual contributions.

=== Novelty ===

The paper is novel in its new branching architecture and provides another application of recurrent world model to offline RL OPE. Otherwise it feels like a fairly plain application of recurrent world model to OPE that seems to obtain better performance. Overall, the novelty is mediocre.

=== Reproduce ===

Maybe reproducible since the authors have provided code.
content.summary_of_the_review:
A few questions regarding the paper.

=== **Motivation** ===

Motivation. Since evaluated envs are Markovian, why is a Markovian world model not enough for offline OPE? I think providing a more clear and detailed investigation into this will greatly boost the motivation for using recurrent models for offline OPE in general. It can just be the case that in practice, using recurrent model is much more superior empirically, but conceptually, it remains unclear why it is the case. Is this because of statistical efficiency? Is this because of these envs are in fact non-Markovian and recurrent model is in fact being useful in a general POMDP setting? 

Overall, the paper has shown good empirical gains over prior methods. But the "why" is not clear. Thus far, I feel general readers cannot gain a better understanding as to why recurrent model is useful in OPE in general. If the paper is meant to just leverage a recurrent model training scheme, most part of which has existed in public, and show it delivers better performance, then the contributions are not novel nor insightful enough.

=== **RSA** ===

The paper proposes that RSA is very important for practical benefits, and has shown evidence through ablation. However, what's not clear to me is why RSA is important specifically in the case of OPE? What is the implication of the RSA loss function that makes the OPE more accurate? 

For example, if RSA benefits recurrent world model in general, what makes the loss function novel in the OPE case? Is this because in addition to the usual training stability benefits provided by RSA in the dreamer setting, extra benefits are present in the OPE case. Or maybe for the offline OPE case, it is even more important to carry out RSA than the dreamer case because now the data is offline.

A clear explanation and motivation for the above question will help elucidate the novelty of the paper's contribution. If RSA does not provide benefits beyond how it helps dreamer, it is not clear if RSA is a novel contribution of the current paper.

=== **Markovian world model** ===

Comparison to Markovian world model. In Fig 3 the paper compares VLBM with auto-regressive world model, obtained from prior work. An experiment to address the conceptual question in Q1 would be to compare with a Markovian world model, and maybe borrow results from prior work if there is any.

=== **Why VLBM is better than AR** ===

Given VLBM and AR are both recurrent world models, a natural question is why one is better than another? It would be nice to have visualizations like in Fig 8 for the AR model too, to see whether it is because AR model fails to distinguish policies with different performance in the representation space.

content.title: Author Response [Part 2]
content.comment:
Q3: Comparison to Markovian world model. In Fig 3 the paper compares VLBM with auto-regressive world model, obtained from prior work. An experiment to address the conceptual question in Q1 would be to compare with a Markovian world model, and maybe borrow results from prior work if there is any.

R3: We appreciate this comment, as we found that in the paper we did not point out that AR is considered Markovian. Specifically, from the AR paper [2], it can be found that the AR model only captures the correlations among different dimensions of the states given the previous state and action, but without temporal correlations over time; thus, it is considered a Markovian model. In other words, it tries to train a model that generates the $i$-th element in $s_t$ conditioned on $s_{t-1}$ and $a_{t-1}$, as well as the 1st to $i-1$-th element of $s_t$ which are already generated iteratively in previous steps following the same schema (any states/actions prior to $t-1$ are not involved), i.e., $f(s_{t}^{(i)}|s_{t}^{(0)}...s_{t}^{(i-1)},a_{t-1},s_{t-1})$ where $s_{t}^{(i)}$ is the $i$-th element of the state vector $s_t$. As a result, the AR model captures $p(s_{t}|s_{t-1},a_{t-1})$ in general and can be considered as Markovian. The results show that VLBM significantly outperforms AR, which justifies the need of using latent models with recurrent components to learn the dynamics.

Q4: Given VLBM and AR are both recurrent world models, a natural question is why one is better than another? It would be nice to have visualizations like in Fig 8 for the AR model too, to see whether it is because AR model fails to distinguish policies with different performance in the representation space.

R4: Since AR model does not have hidden states, nor forms a latent space, we were not able to explicitly capture and visualize the representations it learned. However, from Figures 10 and 11 we found that it does not perform well on Ant- and Halfcheetah- related tasks, which have high state dimensionalities and long horizons respectively. This makes sense since it predicts each dimension of the states recursively and $s_{t+1}$ based on $\hat s_t$ in general, where each prediction is made upon previous model outputs; thus, the error could accumulate over both state dimensions and time horizons. 

We would appreciate the reviewer to follow up with any further comments, or to update the review if the comments above are sufficiently addressed. We sincerely thank the reviewer for the time and patience devoted to the review process.

[2] Zhang, Michael R. et al. "Autoregressive Dynamics Models for Offline Policy Evaluation and Optimization." ICLR 2021.

content.title: Author Response [Part 1]
content.comment:
Thank you for recognizing our empirical contributions and we appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments. Please find our point-by-point response below.

Q1: Since evaluated envs are Markovian, why is a Markovian world model not enough for offline OPE? Is this because of statistical efficiency? Is this because of these envs are in fact non-Markovian and recurrent model is in fact being useful in a general POMDP setting?

R1: Note that the VLBM encodes the transition dynamics in a latent space and uses a recurrent model to enforce the temporal correlations over the latent variables (as shown in Fig.1). Consider that **the latent variables are not necessarily Markovian**, where we use recurrent states to capture the temporal correlations in the latent space. More generally, though the Mujoco and Adroit environments are Markovian, we found that simply fitting the transition function $p(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)$ may not be sufficient. The reason being that during trajectory roll-out, the next state is generated conditioning on the previous state which is also a prediction from the model. As a result, the errors can be propagated recursively over time, which is considered as a major challenge for model-based methods. This had already been justified empirically from results reported in DOPE [1], where the simple feedforward model can lead to 40% (normalized) absolute error on average. 

Q2: The paper proposes that RSA is very important for practical benefits, and has shown evidence through ablation. However, what's not clear to me is why RSA is important specifically in the case of OPE? What is the implication of the RSA loss function that makes the OPE more accurate?

R2: Generally, RSA is designed to resolve the challenge in OPE where the training data only contains **a fixed number of trajectories**, and is collected **fully offline** with **unknown behavioral policies**, as opposed to the latent models used in dreamer/SLAC where new trajectories can be added to the training buffer jointly during training. **The major issue with the VLM dealing with the challenge above is that the encoder and decoder operate independently**--encoder is absent in the generative process (equations 4,5) while decoder is absent from the inference process (equations 2,3). Moreover, both encoder and decoder have their own transitions defined respectively in the latent space, i.e., $q_\psi(z_t|z_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_{t})$ and $p_\phi(z_{t}|z_{t-1},a_t)$. However, **only the KL-divergence terms in the ELBO are responsible for regularizing the latent transitions above** over the entire horizon. A simple summation of these regularization terms over time may not be sufficient for environments with long horizons and limited training data. To resolve this, RSA serves as an additional regularization which tries to align the recurrent states of two types of transitions above, so that the decoder can smoothly tease out the transitions in the latent space (when the encoder is absent) and reconstruct MDP states and rewards. **We also added Appendix B which visualizes the t-SNE over the latent space captured by VLM and VLM+RSA(MSE).** It can be seen that VLM leads to more sparsely distributed latent representations than VLBM. The latent states of VLM+RSA(MSE) distributed almost uniformly, backing up the rationale provided in section 2.4 that MSE could be too strong to regularize the hidden states from the encoder and decoder.

[1] Fu, Justin et al. "Benchmarks for Deep Off-Policy Evaluation." ICLR 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to tackle the Off-Policy Evaluation problem in a model-based fashion, i.e., contrary to importance sampling-based methods, a model is trained to directly generate future trajectories based on past information. The proposed model is a Recurrent Variational Auto-encoder, where both the encoder and decoder are embodied by LSTMs. The main contribution, besides leveraging variational inference for model-based OPE, is the addition of two features: Recurrent State Alignment (RSA) and branching architecture for the decoder.
RSA adds a term in the loss so that the hidden LSTM states of the encoder and the decoder stay close to each other. The authors claim that this term augments the information flow and helps the decoder generate more realistic trajectories.
The branching architecture is a kind of ensemble of decoders, where each branch is assigned a weight (summing to 1 over all branches) that is trained jointly with the parameters of the model. The authors claim that it helps alleviate the effect of initialization.
The authors present results in the DOPE benchmark against model-based and model-free baselines and achieve superior performance overall.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The results on the DOPE benchmark are compelling
- The ablation study is well conducted
- Writing and presentation are pleasant and help get to the point quickly.

Weaknesses:
- The claims and motivation for adding RSA and the branching architecture lack theoretical or empirical justifications, beyond the final results: would it be possible to characterize the behavior observed when MSE is used / RSA is not used, and explain why decoder initialization can lead to such largely decreased performance
- The intuitive statements made by the authors are sometimes vague: would it be possible t clarify terms such as "structure", "information flow" and "impact of initialization artifacts" in this particular context?
- The results might be poorly reliable, as they are given on only 3 random seeds.

Clarity: The paper is well-written overall but motivation is sometimes eluded.

However, the claims and motivation for adding RSA and the branching architecture lack justifications, with some ambiguity in writing at places.

content.title: Author Response [Part 1]
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer's time and efforts on evaluating our work. Please see our response to the comments point-by-point below.

Q1: would it be possible to characterize the behavior observed when MSE is used / RSA is not used, and explain why decoder initialization can lead to such largely decreased performance


R1: *More on RSA empirically.* **In Appendix B we added t-SNE visualizations for the latent space formed by VLM and VLM+RSA (MSE).** It can be seen that state-action pairs are distributed in the latent space captured by VLM much sparsely than VLBM (Fig. 8). Moreover, the latent representations of the state-action pairs captured by VLM+RSA (MSE) are almost uniformly distributed; this is consistent with results in Fig.4 where VLM+RSA (MSE) performs in general worse than VLM, and back up the reasoning provided in section 2.3 that MSE is too strong to regularize the hidden states of encoder and decoder. Such findings illustrate that RSA is important for the encoder to learn a compact and disentangled latent space from which the decoder can sample and reconstruct trajectories meaningfully.

*Illustrate branching empirically.* Fig.6 helped explain how the VLBM benefits from the branching architecture empirically, as it can be observed that most of the branching weights are close to 0 or 1, i.e., only 1-2 (out of 10) branches are assigned with meaningful weights while the others are 'killed'. Consider that all the branches are trained toward the same objective, with the only difference being the initial weights which are initialized randomly. Consequently, such a behavior illustrates that initialization of network weights can impact the performance. **An existing literature [1] also found that deep bayes models are sensitive to random weight initializations.** 

Q2: The intuitive statements made by the authors are sometimes vague: would it be possible t clarify terms such as "structure", "information flow" and "impact of initialization artifacts" in this particular context?


R2: The structural similarity between two vectors is measured by the pairwise RSA loss (7). Unlike MSE which will be zero if and only if the two vectors are exactly the same, pairwise loss can reach to zero even if offsets existed between two vectors, for example, $[1,3,5]$ and $[2,4,6]$. If each vector is plotted out as a line chart, one can observe that any two consecutive elements, across the two charts, follow the same trend in terms of increasing/decreasing; henceforth the structural similarity between two vectors.

'Information flow' originally refers to how the part of decoder $p_\phi(z_t|z_{t-1},a_t)$ can enforce the transitions in latent variables, following the dynamics captured by the part of encoder $p_\psi(z_t|z_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_t)$. From the ELBO (6) it can be seen that the KL-divergence terms are used to regularize these two terms to align with each other, i.e., how the latent transition information captured by $p_\psi(z_t|z_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_t)$ can impact the training of $p_\phi(z_t|z_{t-1},a_t)$. **We have now elaborated on this in sections 2.3 and 2.4, where the changes are highlighted in blue.**

"Impact of initialization artifacts" refers to how random weights initializations would affect the performance of bayes models (parameterized as NNs). **We have removed this term in the paper and spelled it out explicitly as well.**

Q3: The results might be poorly reliable, as they are given on only 3 random seeds.

R3: We followed the guidelines and standardized procedures provided by DOPE, which evaluated each method with 3 random seeds. We also evaluated VLBM and ablations with 3 seeds since this facilitates fair comparison with the baseline results provided in DOPE, to exclude the artifacts/noises that can be possibly brought into baseline results due to the use of hyper-parameters, optimizers etc. Moreover, as mentioned in Appendix A, the estimations from VLBM and ablation baselines are obtained by averaging returns over 50 episodes, as the error is less than 1% across different 50-episode runs. It can be observed that the IS-, DR-, and DICE-based methods could sometimes perform inconsistently across different environments and seeds, while the model-based methods (VLBM and AR) in general show much smaller variations (shorter error bars in Figures 3, 4 and 5, as well as smaller std's in Tables 1-6).

[1] Rossi, Simone et al. "Good initializations of variational bayes for deep models", ICML 2019

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work outlines a model-based approach for off-policy evaluation. It revolves around learning (from a static, offline dataset) a recurrent variational latent model of the environment. They outline two "tricks" to improve the approach. One is termed "recurrent state alignment", an additional loss is used to encourage the hidden state representations in the decoder and the encoder to be similar. Secondly, they use multiple decoders and when using the model for OPE average over the predictions of multiple decoders. They test their approach on some off-policy benchmarks on control tasks and compare with other OPE baselines as well as try ablations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is well-written.

- Off-policy evaluation is an important topic for practical use of RL and of interest to the community.

- Source code is provided.

- The empirical results are compelling.

Weaknesses:
- The environments used (control tasks from D4RL) are typically more used for off policy optimization rather than evaluation. It would be helpful to test the approach on other kinds of OPE tasks such as recommender systems / advertising e.g. [1, 2].

- It would be helpful to discuss (and ideally report experiments) on using this approach for policy optimization rather than just evaluation.

Minor:
- Spelling mistake in section heading 2.

[1] Chen, Minmin, et al. "Off-Policy Actor-critic for Recommender Systems." Proceedings of the 16th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems. 2022.

[2] Saito, Y., Udagawa, T., Kiyohara, H., Mogi, K., Narita, Y., & Tateno, K. (2021, September). Evaluating the robustness of off-policy evaluation. In Fifteenth ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (pp. 114-123).

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer recognizing our contributions. Please see our responses to the comments point-by-point below.

Q1: The environments used (control tasks from D4RL) are typically more used for policy optimization rather than evaluation. It would be helpful to test the approach on other kinds of OPE tasks such as recommender systems / advertising.

R1: We followed the guidelines and standardized procedures introduced in a recent benchmark, DOPE [1], from Levine's group, which provided for each D4RL environment the target policies to be evaluated as well as an off-policy training dataset. We appreciated the reviewer providing additional references, where **we updated the related work section to discuss them (texts highlighted in blue)**. We chose to benchmark above, since a great number of prior OPE works are also tested in Mujoco/Adroit-related environments, such as [2-10], which are published in venues closely related to ICLR.

Q2: It would be helpful to discuss (and ideally report experiments) on using this approach for policy optimization rather than just evaluation.

R2: In this work we specifically focus on OPE as the improvements resulting from the model and loss functions we designed can be isolated, as opposed to policy optimization where the policy improvement step will also impact the performance. Moreover, model-based OPE can facilitate many important applications by itself, such as evaluating how a surgical robot would respond to specific states that are critical to a successful procedure, without deploying it directly to patients. However, this is a great question which points out some of the future research that can build on top of our work. First, one could follow the classic model-based RL methods, which applies model predictive control (MPC), linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) etc. toward the VLBM which serves as a synthetic environment, or if a control policy can be optimized jointly with model training -- similar to the fashion used in dreamer[11]/SLAC[12] but without the need of online interactions with the environment. Further, VLBM even has the potential to replace the critic network in actor-critic methods; given that VLBM can estimate expected total returns accurately, it can be extended to estimate the expected returns starting from specific state-action pairs. **We added such discussions in the conclusion section -- highlighted in blue.** 

Q3: I believe it would be helpful to provide a little more detail (e.g. pseudocode algorithm) on how the model is used for OPE.

R3: Absolutely. We have added Appendix C to introduce more details on this.


Hope we have sufficiently addressed the comments. We would also appreciate the reviewer updating the review score if our work deserves a higher one. Should the reviewer have further comments/follow-ups, we are more than happy to address them.

[2] Zhang, Ruiyi et al. "GenDICE: Generalized Offline Estimation of Stationary Values." ICLR 2020.

[3] Zhang, Shangtong et al. "Gradientdice: Rethinking generalized offline estimation of stationary values." ICLR 2020.

[6] Yang, Mengjiao et al. "Off-policy evaluation via the regularized lagrangian." ICML 2020.

[7] Nachum, Ofir et al. "Dualdice: Behavior-agnostic estimation of discounted stationary distribution corrections." NeurIPS 2019.

[8] Wen, Junfeng et al. "Batch Stationary Distribution Estimation." ICML 2020.

[9] Dai, Bo et al. "Coindice: Off-policy confidence interval estimation." NeurIPS 2020.

Thanks to the authors for responding to my comments.

I concede, as the authors cited their references that D4RL environments are commonly used for OPE benchmarks. However, I still do believe that testing the approach on a wider set of environments would increase the interest in this work. I appreciate them providing comments on how one might apply this approach to policy improvement, however, again I think it would increase the impact and interest in this work to actually try this (but I do agree that just OPE has important applications and many other OPE approaches are not model based).

Overall, I was the most positive reviewer and am still positive about this work (and hence scored for acceptance) but have concerns about the generality and interest in this work.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
Dear Area Chairs and Reviewers,

We appreciate the reviewers' efforts toward providing the invaluable comments. In general, the reviewers recognized that our work is clearly written (MDLU, k3gq, grrh, QLEv), and proposes a novel method (MDLU, k3gq, grrh). Moreover, all reviewers (MDLU, k3gq, grrh, QLEv) deemed that our experimental results are *compelling*, with sufficient ablation studies as well as comparisons against existing baselines that justify the effectiveness of the methodology we introduced.

However, we noticed that some reviewers would prefer us to provide more motivations toward how RSA and branching could help VLBM to tackle the OPE problem conceptually. As a result, we have enriched the discussions at the beginning of sections 2.3 and 2.4 (highlighted in blue), introducing why they are needed and how they impact the training and evaluation of VLBM. Moreover, we have added Appendix B which provide the t-SNE visualizations for two ablation baselines, VLM and VLM+RSA(MSE), to empirically illustrate how RSA and branching can help formulate a more expressive and disentangled latent space. More importantly, as all the reviewers pointed out, the comprehensive ablation studies we conducted serve as a strong empirical justification toward the need of the methodology we proposed.

Below we provided point-by-point responses to address all the questions raised by the reviewers. We would greatly appreciated any follow-ups that facilitate a more comprehensive evaluation of our work.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper proposes a new model-based offline policy evaluation methods. It use a recurrent latent model to learn the world model from offline dataset as a VAE. In order to obtain good performance, it introduces two modifications from vanilla VAE: (1) recurrent state alignment (RSA) that introduces additional regularization to align the latent states in the encoder and decoder; (2) branching architecture that trains multiple models with different parameter initializations. Experiments on the DOPE benchmark shows compelling performance compared to baselines.

Strengths:
- Good empirical performance
- Moderate novelty in the two modifications: RSA and Branching

Weaknesses:
- Not well explained why a recurrent architecture is required for a Markovian environment
- Limited novelty under VAE framework. Not sufficient justification / explanation why the two modifications would help
- (minor) Would be better to consider the proposed recurrent world model in the more general context of offline RL instead of restricted to OPE
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: There are remaining concerns that are not well addressed by the authors' rebuttal.
content.justification_for_why_not_lower_score: Experiments are conducted convincingly and the results are compelling.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting:
Both the strengths and weaknesses were discussed in the meeting.

The main remaining concerns among reviewers were the moderate novelty of the work on top of VAE. The main methodology contributions were recurrent state alignments and branching architecture neither of which had sufficient conceptual justification. Also, it was not clear why a recurrent model would be better than prior works based on the current state for Markovian environments.

Nonetheless, the reviewers consider the empirical results on DOPE were compelling, the paper was well written, and source code was provided to re-reproduction. Some reviewers suggested that there existed methods that did work in practice though were not well justified at the time.

All reviewers consider this paper to be at the borderline with the majority tending to accept the paper.
